deride

/dih-RYD/ - rhymes with ride · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Deride means to mock or laugh at with contempt.

Veteran deckhands deride the yacht club's white gloves and creased trousers every time the launch putters past.

Example

The 1896 etiquette guide gives lady cyclists a full chapter, and the tone is a sneer: it derides the bloomers, the posture, the "wheeled hoyden" herself, and advises gentlemen to keep their bows from any woman met astride a machine. Derision, the chapter shows, needs no argument — contempt and a laugh will carry a page further than a fact.

Deride is the exact word for that chapter, because it means to mock or laugh at with contempt — both parts required. Teasing laughs without the contempt; criticism judges without the laugh. Derision is the laugh that means to shrink you.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

scoff at: To scoff at something is to dismiss it with a quick sneering noise — derision in one syllable, usually aimed at an idea or a claim. Deride goes wider and louder: sustained mockery of a person or thing, with contempt carried in the laughter.

mock: To mock is to make fun of something, often by imitating it — the exaggerated voice, the copied walk. Deride is blunter: open laughter aimed down at its target, with the contempt as the point. Mockery can be sly or theatrical; deride announces the scorn.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

admire: look up at, not down

salute: mark respect out loud

Where it sits · how much contempt the laughter carries — tease → ridicule → deride

tease vs. deride: Tease sits far below deride: tease laughs with its target — affection wearing a grin — while deride laughs at it, meaning to make it smaller.

ridicule vs. deride: Ridicule goes further than tease — the laughter turns public and pointed; deride claims the most: mockery with contempt in it, laughter meant to make its target smaller.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: down

Root — ride-

Root — ride-: to laugh (Latin ridere)

Put it together

Put it together: De- (down) + ridere (to laugh) = to laugh down. Latin deridere was exactly our word: laughter aimed downward at someone. The same laughing root gives ridiculous — "deserving laughter" — and none of this has anything to do with riding; the match with ride is pure accident.

Use the root in a new word: ridiculous

Use the root in a new word: ridiculous: The excuse was so ridiculous that even the friend it was invented for could not repeat it with a straight face.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / sharp

Deride is face-out mockery — it happens in the open, and the contempt is the point. Tease when the laugh is kind; ridicule when it is public but you want the contempt left unsaid. Inside this unit: denigrate works behind the back, deprecate talks worth down without laughing, and deplore would never laugh at all.
